paras: The attempted lynching of Manny Sidebottom took place at Somerset, Kentucky, in April 1888, when a mob gathered to lynch him after he was convicted of murdering Thomas Wilson. The mob stopped to help put out a fire at the Methodist church, and the jailer escaped with his prisoner in the meantime. Papers from Maryland to Louisiana carried the story of the prisoner saved by a church fire.

On March 28, 1888, Tom Wilson of Oliver Springs, Tennessee, was found dead near the Stanford road a mile north of Somerset, his head badly beaten. A Somerset dispatch said Wilson had been seen drinking heavily with a man named Sidebottom the day before, and that "there is talk of lynching him." A second dispatch described Wilson as an old soldier who had come to gather proof for a pension, and said Sidebottom had been arrested and had confessed to killing and robbing him. The headline over that report in a Dakota paper read "They Merely Talk of Lynching."

Sidebottom's trial began at Somerset on a Wednesday in mid-April before a jury summoned from Boyle county. Judge Morrow excluded the confession, and the Boyle jurors later said that without it only circumstantial evidence could be put before them. He was convicted on Friday and sentenced to life imprisonment.

According to the wire report, a mob gathered to lynch Sidebottom while he was being taken to prison. A syndicated account said the mob was on its way to the jail when the Methodist Church caught fire, and its members stopped to help put the fire out. Meanwhile the jailer got word of the mob and left with his prisoner. No one was hurt, and the coverage gives no size or leaders for the mob and no cause for the fire.

No report of arrests or of any official inquiry into the mob appears in the coverage. The Boyle county jurors told a Danville correspondent after they returned home that they did not doubt that Sidebottom deserved hanging. The same column blamed officers who were said to have promised him he could leave the country if he confessed, and defended the judge's ruling.

The episode reached distant papers mainly as a short wire item, which the Daily Republican ran on April 23 and the Democratic Advocate of Westminster, Maryland, repeated on April 28. A longer item calling Wilson "a veteran Federal soldier" ran in early May in the Oxford Eagle, the West Tennessee Star, the Huntsville Gazette and the St. Landry Democrat. These items reported the conviction, the mob and the fire without comment, giving his name as "Manny Sidebottoms."

Closer to home, the Semi-Weekly Interior Journal of Stanford was openly hostile to the prisoner. It wrote that the church fire "is all that saved the miserable murderer, Sidebottom, from having his neck stretched by a mob," and elsewhere called him a "fiendish and cruel murderer." The same paper nonetheless praised Judge Morrow for protecting the rights of "an ignorant individual" and did not call for a lynching. No paper stated Sidebottom's race, and no Black-press account from 1888 is available.

The names vary: the wire and the Stanford paper gave "Manny," while other items gave the initials H. M. or W. H. The murdered man was Thomas or Tom Wilson in the dispatches and wire, but James Wilson in the Stanford paper.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Manny Sidebottom
bases: A mob gathered to lynch a convicted prisoner but was diverted by a church fire before reaching him, a threatened lynching with no one killed (A5, A7, A10).
A mob gathered to lynch Sidebottom for the murder of Thomas Wilson, but the jailer escaped with him and no one was killed (A5, A10); this was a threatened or attempted lynching, not a completed one.
A wire brief (A5) and a separate Kentucky paper (A7) independently report the mob and the church fire, and a fuller syndicated version (A10) agrees.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: After his conviction, a mob gathered to lynch Sidebottom while he was being taken to prison, but stopped to put out a church fire, and the jailer escaped with him.

accounts.label: Syndicated 'few nights ago' item
accounts.gist: The mob was on its way to the jail when the Methodist Church caught fire; it stopped to help, and the jailer, warned, escaped with his prisoner.

accounts.label: Stanford, Ky., paper
accounts.gist: The burning of the Methodist church alone saved Sidebottom from a mob.

framing.detail: The Stanford Interior Journal called him a 'miserable murderer' saved only by the fire, and a 'fiendish and cruel murderer', while also defending Judge Morrow's exclusion of the confession.
Wire and syndicated briefs reported the conviction, mob and fire without comment.
The Yankton paper's headline 'They Merely Talk of Lynching' covered the earlier threat at his arrest.

The Stanford paper says James; dispatches and wire say Thomas.
